outputs.L1: A system and method for configuring monitor blocks and effect blocks associated with a process control system for a process plant include causing a display device to present a graphical user interface indicating a first monitor block, a second monitor block, and an effect block. The system and method further include enabling a user to enter configuration data via an input device, including: (i) configuring one output of the first monitor block to serve as an input to the second monitor block; (ii) configuring an additional output of the first monitor block and an output of the second monitor block to serve as inputs to the effect block; and (iii) designating at least one of the plurality of cells in each of the first monitor block, the second monitor block, and the effect block as a trigger associated with the respective input/output pair for that cell and corresponding to a condition in the process plant.
outputs.L2: A process-plant control system provides a technique for setting up monitor blocks and effect blocks. A display presents a graphical interface showing first and second monitor blocks together with an effect block. Through an input device, a user may enter configuration information that: (i) assigns an output from the first monitor block as an input to the second monitor block; (ii) routes another output from the first monitor block, along with an output from the second monitor block, to inputs of the effect block; and (iii) identifies at least one cell in each of the first monitor block, second monitor block, and effect block as a trigger linked to that cell’s corresponding input/output pair and to a particular condition within the process plant.
outputs.L3:
The system enables users to configure monitor blocks and effect blocks within a process control system for a process plant. Through a graphical user interface, the system displays a first monitor block, a second monitor block, and an effect block, allowing users to define relationships among the blocks.

A user may configure an output of the first monitor block as an input to the second monitor block, thereby creating a monitoring sequence or dependency. The user may also configure outputs from both the first and second monitor blocks as inputs to the effect block. In this arrangement, the effect block can respond to information generated by either or both monitor blocks.

Each block includes one or more configurable cells. At least one cell in each block may be designated as a trigger associated with a particular input/output pair and a specified condition in the process plant. When the associated plant condition is detected, the trigger can activate the corresponding input/output relationship, enabling the configured blocks to monitor plant operations and initiate an appropriate effect.
outputs.L4:
A process-control configuration system provides a graphical user interface for defining relationships among monitoring and response components within a process plant. Through the interface, a user can select a first monitor block, identify one or more outputs produced by that block, and connect those outputs to corresponding inputs of a second monitor block and an effect block. The graphical representation may use cells, nodes, lines, or other visual elements to show the configured data and control paths.

The first monitor block observes selected process variables, equipment states, alarms, or other plant conditions. Its outputs can represent measured values, calculated values, status indicators, or Boolean condition signals. By connecting an output of the first monitor block to an input of the second monitor block, the user enables the second block to evaluate the output in combination with other information. This arrangement supports layered or coordinated monitoring, such as determining whether several related conditions exist at the same time.

The interface also allows selected cells to be designated as condition-based triggers. A trigger cell defines a condition that must be satisfied before an associated operation or response is initiated. Such a condition may be based on a threshold, a change in state, a combination of monitor outputs, or another logical expression. The user can configure the trigger directly within the graphical environment, making the relationship between the monitored condition and the resulting action readily visible.

An output from the first monitor block, the second monitor block, or both may be connected to an input of an effect block. The effect block represents a response to the detected plant condition, such as generating an alarm, issuing a notification, recording an event, changing a control parameter, initiating a procedure, or commanding plant equipment. Each connection is established through a defined output/input pair so that the source of the information and its intended destination are clearly specified.

Once the configuration is complete, the system stores the block definitions, trigger designations, and input/output mappings as an executable or deployable control configuration. During operation, the monitor blocks evaluate process-plant data and pass their outputs along the configured connections. When the designated trigger conditions are met, the effect block performs the assigned response.

In this manner, the configuration system enables users to create coordinated monitoring and response strategies without manually programming each relationship. The graphical interface makes dependencies among process conditions, monitor blocks, trigger cells, and effect blocks easier to define, review, and modify, while the use of explicit input/output pairs promotes consistent and reliable operation throughout the process-control environment.
outputs.L5:
### The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the smallest and most frequently used words in the English language. Though it may seem insignificant, it plays an essential role in communication. As the definite article, “the” points to a specific person, place, object, or idea. For example, “a book” can mean any book, while “the book” refers to one that is already known or clearly identified.

Beyond grammar, “the” helps create shared understanding. Phrases such as “the sun,” “the future,” and “the truth” suggest something unique or universally recognizable. Without this simple word, many sentences would become vague or unnatural.

Small words often have great importance, and “the” is a perfect example. Quietly and consistently, it brings precision, clarity, and structure to the English language.

counterfactuals.output: A system and method are disclosed for graphically configuring monitoring and control functionality in a process plant. A graphical configuration interface presents a workspace in which a user selects, places, and interconnects monitor blocks and effect blocks. Each monitor block receives or evaluates one or more process parameters to detect a process condition, while each effect block specifies an action to be performed in response to the detected condition. Graphical links define signal, status, logic, or execution relationships among the blocks and may include configurable attributes, conditions, priorities, or delays. The system validates block compatibility, connection integrity, parameter assignments, and execution dependencies, and generates an executable configuration from the graphical representation. The executable configuration may be downloaded to one or more controllers, field devices, servers, or other process plant nodes for distributed execution. During operation, the interface may display live process values, block states, alarms, and effect status in association with the graphical configuration, thereby facilitating configuration, testing, diagnostics, modification, and maintenance of interconnected process monitoring and response functions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an invention in formal patent language where a GUI allows a user to connect an output of a first monitor block to a second monitor block, route outputs from both monitor blocks into an effect block, and designate trigger cells.
counterfactuals.output:
### Abstract

A computer-implemented system provides a graphical user interface for configuring a signal-processing arrangement. The graphical user interface displays a first monitor block, a second monitor block, and an effect block within a workspace comprising a plurality of user-selectable cells. The system receives user input connecting an output of the first monitor block to an input of the second monitor block and further receives user input routing respective outputs of the first and second monitor blocks to the effect block. One or more cells of the workspace may be designated as trigger cells. Activation of a trigger cell causes the system to initiate, modify, or terminate monitoring or effect-processing operations associated with one or more of the displayed blocks.

### Exemplary Independent Claim

1. **A computer-implemented method**, comprising:  
   presenting, by a computing device, a graphical user interface including a first monitor block, a second monitor block, an effect block, and a plurality of cells;

   receiving, through the graphical user interface, a first user input defining a connection between an output of the first monitor block and an input of the second monitor block;

   receiving, through the graphical user interface, one or more second user inputs defining respective signal routes from the output of the first monitor block and an output of the second monitor block to one or more inputs of the effect block;

   receiving a third user input designating at least one of the plurality of cells as a trigger cell;

   storing configuration data representative of the connection, the respective signal routes, and the designation of the trigger cell; and

   in response to activation of the trigger cell, controlling execution of at least one operation associated with the first monitor block, the second monitor block, or the effect block in accordance with the stored configuration data.

### Exemplary Dependent Claims

2. The method of claim 1, wherein the first user input comprises a drag-and-drop operation extending a graphical connector from an output port of the first monitor block to an input port of the second monitor block.

3. The method of claim 1, wherein the effect block combines or independently processes signals received from the respective outputs of the first and second monitor blocks.

4. The method of claim 1, wherein designation of the trigger cell includes associating the trigger cell with a condition, event, user command, timing value, or monitored signal state.

5. The method of claim 1, further comprising visually distinguishing the trigger cell from non-trigger cells by at least one of color, shading, iconography, animation, or boundary formatting.

6. The method of claim 1, wherein activation of the trigger cell causes the effect block to apply a selected effect parameter to at least one signal received from the first or second monitor block.

7. The method of claim 1, further comprising validating the connection and the respective signal routes based on port compatibility rules and presenting an error indication when a proposed connection violates the port compatibility rules.

8. The method of claim 1, wherein the graphical user interface dynamically displays signal-flow indicators along the connection and the respective signal routes during execution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical summary of a method for configuring cause-and-effect logic in an industrial process control system using graphical monitor and effect blocks with cell-based triggers.
counterfactuals.output:
### Technical Summary

The method configures cause-and-effect logic in an industrial process control system through a graphical matrix composed of **monitor blocks**, **effect blocks**, and configurable **trigger cells**.

- **Monitor blocks** represent process conditions or causes, such as high pressure, low flow, equipment failure, or operator commands. Each block receives one or more field or controller signals and evaluates them using configured thresholds, states, delays, quality checks, and latching rules.
- **Effect blocks** represent control responses, including valve closure, pump shutdown, alarm generation, permissive removal, or initiation of a shutdown sequence.
- The graphical interface arranges causes and effects along separate matrix axes. Each intersecting **cell** defines the logical relationship between a monitor block and an effect block.

A cell is configured with a trigger type or state—for example, active-high, active-low, bypassed, latched, delayed, or unused. When a monitor block detects its configured condition, the system evaluates all associated cells. Active cells transmit trigger states to the corresponding effect blocks. Each effect block combines incoming triggers using configured voting or Boolean logic, such as OR, AND, *M-out-of-N*, inhibit, or reset logic, and then issues the designated control action.

Configuration data is converted into executable controller logic or runtime parameters while retaining the graphical matrix as the engineering representation. The system may validate signal references, detect incomplete or conflicting mappings, enforce safety constraints, and support online monitoring. During operation, the display can indicate active causes, asserted cells, triggered effects, bypasses, and latched states, enabling operators and engineers to trace an action from the initiating process condition to the resulting control response.

This approach provides a compact, auditable way to configure interlocks, trips, alarms, and safety sequences without manually constructing each Boolean connection, while maintaining deterministic execution and clear cause-to-effect traceability.
